docs.title: Calculate RPW
docs.text: Calculate RPW is a cross-platform, offline assembly line balancing calculator built with Flutter and Material 3. It implements the Helgeson and Birnie Ranked Positional Weight (RPW) method for Android (phones, foldables, tablets, and Wear OS), Web browsers, and Windows.

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
• Dual Input Modes: Use the Guided Form to enter connections, task times, and cycle time visually, or switch to Quick Text Mode for fast space-separated entry.
  • Built-in Examples: Load textbook 6-node, 8-node parallel, or oversized-task edge cases with one tap.
  • Complete Balancing Metrics: Computes arrow chains, ranked RPW priority tables, balanced workstations, station idle times, balance delay, line efficiency, and production rate.
  • Adaptive Material 3 UI: Responds smoothly to window resizing, foldable hinges, display cutouts, multi-window layouts, and Wear OS screens.
  • Offline and Private: Zero tracking, zero telemetry, and zero Android permissions required.

docs.title: Privacy Policy
docs.text: Calculate RPW runs entirely offline on your device. No personal information, assembly line inputs, or telemetry ever leave your device.

docs.title: Data Collection
docs.text: We do not collect, transmit, store remotely, or share any personal data, location data, usage analytics, advertising identifiers, or crash reports.

docs.title: Local Preferences and Permissions
docs.text:
• Android Permissions: The Android release build declares zero special permissions and does not request internet access.
  • On-Device Storage: Only your selected theme mode (System, Light, or Dark) is saved locally via standard platform preferences.
  • Clipboard: The app writes to your clipboard only when you tap a result card or press Copy Report.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: Calculate RPW helps industrial engineers, operations students, and manufacturing teams balance assembly lines by grouping tasks into workstations without exceeding a target cycle time.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text:
• Node: A numbered work element in your assembly sequence (1, 2, 3, and so on).
  • Tek: Time required to finish a single work element (zero or positive).
  • Precedence Edge (From -> To): Dependency showing that the From task must finish before the To task starts.
  • Final Node: Terminal task where all precedence paths converge.
  • Cycle Time: Maximum allowed workload per workstation.
  • RPW (Ranked Positional Weight): Sum of a task's own Tek plus the Tek of every downstream task reachable from it.
  • Balance Delay: Idle fraction across all stations relative to total station capacity.
  • Production Rate: Output rate given by 1 / maxStationLoad units per minute.

docs.title: Guided Form Mode
docs.text:
1. Select Guided Form at the top of the calculator (or choose a preset from Quick Examples).
  2. Enter From, To, and the From node's Tek, then select Add.
  3. Enter the Final Node, Final Tek, and target Cycle Time.
  4. Select Calculate to generate workstation assignments, RPW rankings, arrow chains, and efficiency metrics.
  5. Tap any result card to copy that entry, or select Copy Report to copy the full summary.

docs.title: Quick Text Mode
docs.text:
Switch to Quick Text for keyboard-driven entry with spaces:

  1. Enter total number of connections (for example 6).
  2. Enter each connection as From To Tek (for example 1 2 0.4).
  3. Enter FinalNode Tek (for example 6 0.4).
  4. Enter CycleTime (for example 1.0). Calculation starts automatically after step 4.

docs.title: Worked 6-Node Example
docs.text:
• Edges: 1 2 0.4, 1 3 0.4, 2 4 0.6, 3 4 0.3, 4 5 0.5, 5 6 0.2
  • Final node and Tek: 6 0.4
  • Cycle time: 1.0
  • Balanced output:
  • Station 1: N1, N2 (Load 1.0, Idle 0)
  • Station 2: N3, N4, N5 (Load 1.0, Idle 0)
  • Station 3: N6 (Load 0.4, Idle 0.6)
  • Balance Delay: 20% (0.2), Line Efficiency: 80%, Production Rate: 1 units/min

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records
docs.text:
This directory tracks major architectural decisions made during the modernization of Calculate RPW using the Michael Nygard ADR format.

Number Title Status 0001 Layered MVVM Architecture and State Management Accepted 0002 Platform-Agnostic Design and Adaptive Material 3 UI Accepted 0003 Android AGP 9 Built-in Kotlin and SDK 37 Target Accepted 0004 RPW Domain Logic Bug Fixes and Input Validation Accepted 0005 Offline-First Privacy and Zero-Permission Policy Accepted

docs.title: 1. Layered MVVM Architecture and State Management
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The legacy application kept UI widgets, input validation, mutable calculation arrays, and the RPW solver inside a single stateful widget (Home.dart). This tight coupling made unit testing impossible, risked state leaks across runs, and mixed platform clipboard and theme logic directly with domain math.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Adopt a clean layered architecture organized into core, domain, data, app, and ui:

  • Keep lib/domain/ strictly pure Dart with zero Flutter or platform dependencies.
  • Apply clear design patterns where they fit naturally:
  • Strategy (RpwSolver and HelgesonBirnieRpwSolver)
  • Factory (SampleProblemFactory)
  • Singleton (ServiceLocator with test reset support)
  • Composite (ResultNode, ResultGroup, and ResultItem)
  • Use standard ChangeNotifier ViewModels (CalculatorViewModel) and Repositories (ThemeRepository) wired via Provider, paired with go_router (StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack) for declarative routing.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Domain algorithms, validation rules, and ViewModel transitions can be verified directly with fast unit tests.
  • Replacing storage, clipboard, or solver implementations requires only swapping an injected interface in ServiceLocator.
  • Contributors must keep business calculations inside lib/domain/ rather than UI widget state.

docs.title: 2. Platform-Agnostic Design and Adaptive Material 3 UI
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The legacy app used Material 2 theming (primarySwatch, headline6), relied on older third-party packages (theme_provider, clipboard, flutter_fadein), and scaled a single vertical column only by raw MediaQuery width divisions. Modern deployments must work well across phones (compact to large), foldables, tablets, Wear OS watches, resizable multi-window desktop panes, and Web browsers without platform-specific forks in business or UI logic.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Upgrade UI imports to package:material_ui/material_ui.dart and Material 3 (ColorScheme.fromSeed).
  • Drive every responsive transition from LayoutBuilder constraints via WindowSizeClass breakpoints (wear under 300dp, compact, medium, expanded, and large) rather than checking device OS or locking screen orientation.
  • Support foldable hinges and display cutouts using SafeArea, edge-to-edge system chrome, DisplayFeatureSubScreen, and android:windowLayoutInDisplayCutoutMode = shortEdges.
  • Replace legacy clipboard and theme packages with Flutter's built-in Clipboard API and shared_preferences, ensuring identical Dart code runs on Android, Web, and Windows.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Layouts adapt smoothly when windows resize, split screens activate, or foldables unfold.
  • Removing legacy third-party UI dependencies shrinks dependency surface and eliminates null-safety and platform compatibility drift.
  • Wear OS users receive a streamlined preset-driven view instead of cramped multi-column text inputs.

docs.title: 3. Android AGP 9 Built-in Kotlin and SDK 37 Target
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The project's Android build used legacy Groovy scripts (build.gradle), Gradle 5.6.2, AGP 3.5.0, Kotlin 1.3.50, compileSdkVersion 29, targetSdkVersion 29, and deprecated jcenter() / Jetifier settings. Google Play requires targeting recent Android SDK releases, and modern Flutter toolchains expect Kotlin DSL (*.kts), Java 17 bytecode, and AGP 9 built-in Kotlin support.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Migrate all Android Gradle scripts to Kotlin DSL (settings.gradle.kts, build.gradle.kts, app/build.gradle.kts).
  • Upgrade the Gradle wrapper to 9.5.0 and Android Gradle Plugin to 9.3.1.
  • Target compileSdk = 37, targetSdk = 37, and minSdk = 24.
  • Remove the external org.jetbrains.kotlin.android plugin and rely on AGP 9 built-in Kotlin (kotlin { compilerOptions { jvmTarget = JvmTarget.JVM_17 } }).
  • Enable R8 shrinking and resource shrinking (isMinifyEnabled = true, isShrinkResources = true) with ProGuard keep rules for Flutter embedding.
  • Remove deprecated android.enableJetifier and android.enableR8 properties, and move MainActivity to com.makeshtech.rpw.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Release APKs and AABs satisfy modern Google Play SDK and R8 optimization requirements.
  • Dropping the standalone Kotlin Gradle plugin avoids AGP 9 plugin conflicts and reduces build script boilerplate.
  • Note: If Flutter's Gradle plugin triggers DisableNewDslMigration, android.newDsl=false may be retained in gradle.properties solely until Flutter removes legacy AGP DSL hooks; android.builtInKotlin remains enabled.

docs.title: 4. RPW Domain Logic Bug Fixes and Input Validation
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
An audit of the legacy RPW calculation in Home.dart uncovered five correctness and availability issues:

  1. rangeOut.contains(nodeId) compared integer IDs against List rows (always false) while shadowing loop index i, causing an infinite freeze whenever a downstream node depended on an oversized task (Tek > cycleTime) or when graphs contained cycles.
  2. getArrowChain exited early on hitting finalNodeId, skipping subsequent outgoing branches from the same source node.
  3. RPW values were matched to sorted node rows by list position instead of node ID, scrambling results whenever finalNodeId was not numerically largest.
  4. maxRPW ignored rangeOut stations, allowing division by zero or negative balance delay; Production Rate was also printed to console instead of shown in the UI.
  5. clearAll() omitted several internal lists and fields, leaking stale edges into subsequent runs.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Keep the Helgeson and Birnie RPW workflow and output steps intact while fixing all five defects inside HelgesonBirnieRpwSolver, RpwInputValidator, and CalculatorViewModel:

  • Validate inputs against OWASP allowlists and safe size caps (maxEdges = 500, maxUniqueNodes = 200), rejecting self-loops, duplicates, conflicting Tek values, cycles, and disconnected graphs before solving.
  • Traverse forward arrow chains using a visited set without premature break statements.
  • Store tekByNode and rpwByNode keyed strictly by integer node ID.
  • Track rangeOutIds and dependsOnBigIds explicitly with a forward-progress guard so workstation packing always terminates.
  • Compute maxStationLoad across all workstations, guard zero denominators, and display Production Rate in the UI alongside Balance Delay and Line Efficiency.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every valid and invalid input terminates deterministically in bounded time and memory.
  • Users receive clear validation errors rather than silent miscalculations or app freezes.
  • Regression tests in test/domain/services/rpw_solver_test.dart lock in each fix.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Calculate RPW is distributed publicly via Google Play Console and GitHub Pages. Industrial engineering calculations often involve internal cycle times and line structures, and users expect a pure calculator utility to request zero invasive permissions and transmit no telemetry.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Strip all <uses-permission> declarations from android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml, retaining INTERNET only in debug and profile manifests for Flutter tooling.
  • Set android:allowBackup="false", android:usesCleartextTraffic="false", and android:taskAffinity="" in the Android manifest.
  • Store no user inputs on disk; persist only the chosen ThemeMode locally via SharedPreferencesAsync.
  • Include an in-app Privacy screen and publish a standalone static privacy page at /privacy/ on GitHub Pages for Google Play Console compliance.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The production Android package requests zero runtime or install-time permissions.
  • No third-party analytics SDKs, network clients, or data-collection disclosures are required.
  • Google Play Console reviewers and end users can verify the privacy commitment directly at the static /privacy/ URL.
